alt: Absorption by leaf pigments and rate of photosynthesis against wavelength: both are highest in blue-violet light (95% and 90% at 450 nm) and red light (80% and 85% at 650 nm), and lowest in green light (12% and 25% at 550 nm) and at 700 nm, so the action spectrum follows the absorption spectrum.
caption: Figure: absorption spectrum and action spectrum from the lesson's table (illustrative values)

alt: Action potential trace from the worked solution: resting potential −70 mV, rising past the −55 mV threshold to a peak of +35 mV at 1.0 ms as sodium ions enter, then falling as potassium ions leave through −65 mV at 2.0 ms to a hyperpolarisation of −80 mV at 2.5 ms and back to −70 mV by 4.0 ms.
caption: Figure: an action potential at one point on an axon, with the ion movements that cause each phase

alt: Aerobic respiration in four stages with counts per glucose: glycolysis in the cytoplasm gives 2 pyruvate, 2 net ATP and 2 reduced NAD; the link reaction and Krebs cycle (each twice) in the matrix give 6 CO2, 8 more reduced NAD, 2 reduced FAD and 2 ATP; oxidative phosphorylation on the inner membrane makes 25 + 3 = 28 ATP, so the total is 4 + 28 = 32 ATP.
caption: Figure: the four stages of aerobic respiration and the yield per glucose (values from the worked solutions)

alt: Labelled animal cell as seen with an electron microscope: the nucleus has a double envelope with pores and a dark nucleolus; rough ER with ribosomes lies near the nucleus, a Golgi stack and lysosome sit towards the cell surface membrane, mitochondria have folded cristae, and centrioles and free 80S ribosomes lie in the cytoplasm.
caption: Figure: a generalised animal cell showing the organelles named in the lesson

alt: Antibody concentration after two exposures to the same antigen: after the first exposure on day 0 it peaks slowly at 20 units on day 14 and falls to 3 by day 28; after the second exposure on day 28 it rises faster to 150 by day 35 and peaks at 380 on day 42, 19 times the first peak, then falls more slowly, showing the effect of memory cells.
caption: Figure: primary and secondary immune responses, from the lesson's data (exposures on day 0 and day 28)

alt: Labelled bacterium: a capsule and a peptidoglycan cell wall lie outside the cell surface membrane; inside, circular DNA lies free in the cytoplasm with no nuclear envelope, with small plasmid rings, 70S ribosomes and no membrane-bound organelles; pili and a flagellum project from the surface.
caption: Figure: structure of a typical bacterium (a prokaryote), about 1 to 5 micrometres long

alt: Blood glucose after a meal: 5.0 mmol per dm3 at the start rises 50% to a peak of 7.5 at 30 min, then falls through 6.6 and 5.6 to 5.0 at 120 min and dips slightly to 4.9 at 150 min, fluctuating around the set point as negative feedback corrects it.
caption: Figure: blood glucose after a meal, from the worked solution

alt: Calvin cycle with the counts for one hexose: 6 CO2 combine with 6 RuBP (5C) to give 12 GP (3C); 12 GP are reduced to 12 TP using 12 ATP and 12 reduced NADP; 10 TP are used with 6 ATP to regenerate 6 RuBP, and the other 2 TP leave to make one hexose; the total cost is 18 ATP and 12 reduced NADP.
caption: Figure: the Calvin cycle with the numbers for making one hexose (worked solution)

alt: Pressure in the left atrium, left ventricle and aorta over one 0.8 s cardiac cycle: ventricular pressure jumps from 1.2 to 15.0 kPa between 0.1 and 0.2 s and peaks at 16.0 kPa at 0.3 s, above the aortic 14.5 to 15.5 kPa so the semilunar valve opens; by 0.4 s the ventricle (8.0) is below the aorta (13.2) and it shuts, while aortic pressure never falls below 10.7 kPa.
caption: Figure: pressure changes in the left side of the heart during one cycle (data from the worked solution)

alt: DNA content per cell through a 20-hour cell cycle: it stays at 1 unit through G1 (9 h), doubles to 2 units during S phase (7 h), stays at 2 through G2 (3 h) and mitosis (1 h), then falls back to 1 unit in each daughter cell after cytokinesis.
caption: Figure: DNA content during the cell cycle, with phase lengths from the worked example (9 + 7 + 3 + 1 = 20 h)

alt: Cholinergic synapse: an action potential arrives at the presynaptic knob, voltage-gated calcium channels open and Ca2+ enters, vesicles of acetylcholine fuse with the membrane and release ACh into the 20 nm cleft, ACh binds to receptors that are sodium channels in the postsynaptic membrane so Na+ enters and depolarises it, and acetylcholinesterase breaks the ACh down so its products return to the knob.
caption: Figure: transmission across a cholinergic synapse, in the six numbered steps

alt: DNA fragment drawn as a ladder: the top strand 5' ATGCCGTA 3' pairs with the antiparallel bottom strand 3' TACGGCAT 5' by hydrogen bonds, two for each A-T pair and three for each C-G pair, so the four A-T and four C-G pairs give 8 + 12 = 20 hydrogen bonds; sugar-phosphate backbones run along the outside.
caption: Figure: complementary base pairing in an eight-base-pair fragment (the worked example), with hydrogen bonds counted

alt: Replication fork: the parental double helix on the right is unwound by helicase; on the upper template the leading strand is built continuously towards the fork by DNA polymerase, while on the lower template the lagging strand is built away from the fork as short Okazaki fragments that ligase later joins; DNA polymerase adds nucleotides only in the 5' to 3' direction.
caption: Figure: the replication fork, showing why one new strand is continuous and the other is made in fragments

alt: Rate against substrate concentration for an enzyme: with no inhibitor the curve levels towards a Vmax of 0.80 and reaches half Vmax (0.40) at Km 2 mmol per dm3; competitive inhibitor P reaches the same Vmax but its Km rises to about 5; non-competitive inhibitor Q levels off at only 0.40 with Km still 2.
caption: Figure: Michaelis-Menten curves from the worked data; a competitive inhibitor raises Km, a non-competitive one lowers Vmax

alt: Fluid-mosaic model: a phospholipid bilayer with hydrophilic heads facing the watery outside and inside and hydrophobic tails in the middle, with cholesterol between the tails, a channel protein and a carrier protein spanning the bilayer, extrinsic proteins on the surfaces, and glycoproteins and glycolipids carrying carbohydrate chains on the outer surface.
caption: Figure: the fluid-mosaic model of the cell surface membrane

alt: Glucose tolerance test: person A starts at 4.8 mmol per dm3, peaks at 7.6 at 30 minutes and is back to 5.0 by 120 minutes; person B starts higher at 7.2, peaks at 15.1 at 60 minutes and is still 12.6 at 120 minutes, a pattern consistent with diabetes.
caption: Figure: glucose tolerance test for two adults, from the lesson's table

alt: Hardy-Weinberg genotype frequencies against the frequency q of the recessive allele: p squared falls from 1 to 0, 2pq peaks at 0.5 when q is 0.5, and q squared rises from 0 to 1; at q = 0.2 (the snails) the frequencies are 0.64, 0.32 and 0.04, and at q = 0.3 (the cattle) 0.49, 0.42 and 0.09.
caption: Figure: Hardy-Weinberg genotype frequencies, with the snail and cattle populations marked

alt: Internal structure of the heart: deoxygenated blood from the venae cavae enters the right atrium and passes through the tricuspid valve to the right ventricle and out by the pulmonary artery; oxygenated blood from the pulmonary veins enters the left atrium, passes through the bicuspid valve to the left ventricle, whose wall is two to three times thicker, and leaves by the aorta; a septum separates the two sides and tendinous cords hold the valve flaps.
caption: Figure: the four chambers, valves and main vessels of the mammalian heart (diagrammatic)

alt: Light-dependent stage in the thylakoid membrane: light excites electrons in photosystem II, water is split in the thylakoid space to give protons, electrons and oxygen, electrons pass along carriers to photosystem I and then to NADP in the stroma to make reduced NADP, protons pumped into the thylakoid space flow back through ATP synthase to make ATP.
caption: Figure: non-cyclic photophosphorylation, with electron flow, proton pumping and chemiosmosis

alt: Rate of photosynthesis against light intensity at two carbon dioxide concentrations: both curves rise together up to about 10 units, so light is limiting; the 0.04% CO2 curve levels off at 24 by about 40 units, where CO2 is limiting, while the 0.10% CO2 curve rises further and levels off at 48.
caption: Figure: limiting factors, from the lesson's table (temperature kept at 25 °C)

alt: Meiosis in a cell with 2n = 4: in prophase I homologous chromosomes pair into bivalents and cross over at chiasmata; in metaphase I the bivalents lie on the equator; in anaphase I whole homologues separate, giving two cells with n = 2 and double chromosomes; meiosis II separates the sister chromatids, giving four haploid cells with single chromosomes.
caption: Figure: meiosis I separates homologous chromosomes, meiosis II separates sister chromatids

alt: Meselson and Stahl result: after growth in heavy nitrogen the DNA forms one low heavy band; after one generation in light nitrogen it forms one intermediate hybrid band; after two generations there are equal hybrid and light bands; after three generations 2 of 8 molecules are hybrid and 6 of 8 are light. Only semi-conservative replication predicts all of these.
caption: Figure: DNA bands in the Meselson-Stahl experiment (band thickness shows the proportion of molecules)

alt: Two double-membrane organelles side by side: a mitochondrion with a smooth outer membrane, an inner membrane folded into cristae and a matrix holding Krebs cycle enzymes, and a chloroplast whose thylakoids are stacked in grana inside a stroma where the Calvin cycle occurs.
caption: Figure: mitochondrion and chloroplast, each with a double membrane and its own 70S ribosomes and circular DNA

alt: Four stages of mitosis in a cell with 2n = 4: in prophase the double chromosomes condense and the nuclear envelope breaks down; in metaphase they line up on the equator attached to spindle fibres; in anaphase the sister chromatids are pulled apart to opposite poles; in telophase two nuclei reform and the cell pinches in two, giving identical cells.
caption: Figure: the stages of mitosis (spindle fibres drawn as thin grey lines)

alt: Monohybrid cross for tall (T) and dwarf (t) peas: pure-breeding TT × tt gives all Tt (tall) in F1; crossing two F1 plants gives a Punnett square with TT, Tt, Tt and tt, so the genotype ratio is 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt and the phenotype ratio is 3 tall : 1 dwarf.
caption: Figure: the tall × dwarf cross to F2, with the Punnett square for Tt × Tt

alt: Negative feedback loop: a change in a factor away from its set point is detected by receptors, passed to a control centre, which triggers effectors, producing a response that reverses the change so the factor returns towards the set point; as it returns the stimulus is reduced and so the response is reduced.
caption: Figure: the parts of a negative feedback control system

alt: Nephron and collecting duct: blood enters the glomerulus in the cortex by the wider afferent arteriole and leaves by the narrower efferent arteriole; filtrate passes from Bowman's capsule along the proximal convoluted tubule, down the descending limb and up the ascending limb of the loop of Henle in the medulla, through the distal convoluted tubule and into a collecting duct that runs down to the renal pelvis.
caption: Figure: one nephron, showing which parts lie in the cortex and which in the medulla

alt: Nitrogen cycle: nitrogen gas is fixed to ammonium by Rhizobium, free-living bacteria, lightning and the Haber process; Nitrosomonas turns ammonium into nitrite and Nitrobacter turns nitrite into nitrate; plants take up nitrate and make proteins, animals eat plants, and dead organisms, urea and faeces are ammonified back to ammonium; denitrifying bacteria in waterlogged soil turn nitrate back to nitrogen gas.
caption: Figure: the nitrogen cycle and the bacteria involved at each stage

alt: Oxygen dissociation curves of adult haemoglobin: both are S-shaped and nearly flat at 97% (low CO2) and 95% (high CO2) at 12 kPa in the lungs; at 4 kPa in a muscle saturation is 60% at low CO2 but only 45% at high CO2, so the Bohr shift to the right unloads more oxygen.
caption: Figure: S-shaped oxygen dissociation curves at low and high carbon dioxide (data from the worked solution)

alt: Pedigree of the family with haemophilia: the grandmother I-2 is a carrier, her son II-1 is affected, her daughter II-2 is a carrier who has two sons with the unaffected father II-3; one son, III-2, has haemophilia (XhY) and the other is unaffected. The condition passes through carrier females and affects males.
caption: Figure: pedigree for an X-linked recessive condition (haemophilia), matching the family history described

alt: Chromatogram with a solvent front 80 mm from the origin: carotene moved 76 mm (Rf 0.95), xanthophyll 59 mm (Rf 0.74), chlorophyll a 51 mm (Rf 0.64) and chlorophyll b 36 mm (Rf 0.45); every Rf is below 1 and the most soluble pigment, carotene, travels furthest.
caption: Figure: separation of leaf pigments by chromatography, with Rf = distance moved by spot ÷ distance moved by solvent

alt: Bubble potometer: a leafy shoot cut under water is fixed with an airtight bung into a water-filled tube joined to a horizontal capillary with a scale and an air bubble; as the shoot takes up water the bubble moves along the scale, and with a bore radius of 0.5 mm a movement of 42 mm in 5 minutes means 33.0 mm3 of water, or 6.60 mm3 per minute.
caption: Figure: a bubble potometer and the calculation of the rate of water uptake from the distance moved

alt: Root cross-section from soil to xylem: water enters the root hair cell and crosses the cortex by the apoplast pathway along cell walls, the symplast pathway through cytoplasm and plasmodesmata and the vacuolar pathway through vacuoles; at the endodermis the Casparian strip blocks the apoplast route so water must pass through the cell surface membrane before reaching the xylem.
caption: Figure: the three pathways for water across the root cortex, and the Casparian strip in the endodermis

alt: Potentials in kPa from soil to xylem: soil water −30 (solute −30, pressure 0); root hair cell −340 (−620 + 280); cortex cell −400 (−700 + 300); xylem sap −550 (−150 + −400). Water potential falls steadily inwards, so water moves by osmosis down the gradient, and the negative pressure in the xylem shows tension.
caption: Figure: solute, pressure and water potential at four places across a root (values from the worked solution)

alt: A sarcomere at three lengths with myosin 1.6 µm and actin 1.0 µm long: at 2.4 µm the I band is 0.8 µm and the H zone 0.4 µm; at 2.2 µm they are 0.6 and 0.2 µm; at 2.0 µm the I band is 0.4 µm and the H zone has gone, while the A band stays 1.6 µm because the filaments slide but do not shorten.
caption: Figure: the sliding filament model; the A band stays the same while the I band and H zone shorten

alt: Soil nitrate after flooding: it falls steeply from 24 to 18, 11 and 6 mg per kg over the first six days and then more slowly to 4 and 3 mg per kg by day 10, a total decrease of 87.5%, because waterlogged soil favours denitrifying bacteria.
caption: Figure: soil nitrate after flooding, from the lesson's table

alt: Mean stomatal aperture through a hot sunny day: about 0.5 micrometres at 04:00, opening to a maximum of 8.0 at 10:00, falling to 4.0 at 14:00 as water stress closes some stomata, rising again to 5.5 at 16:00, then closing to 0.5 by 20:00.
caption: Figure: stomatal aperture through the day, from the lesson's table

alt: Transcription of the worked example: the template strand 3' TACCGGAAGCTTATT 5' is read by RNA polymerase and free RNA nucleotides pair with it, giving mRNA 5' AUGGCCUUCGAAUAA 3' (A pairs with U, T with A, C with G, G with C); the codons AUG GCC UUC GAA UAA specify Met, Ala, Phe, Glu and a stop signal.
caption: Figure: the mRNA made from a template strand, split into codons (the worked example)

alt: Translation of the worked-example mRNA 5' AUG AAA GCU UGG CAU UAG 3': a ribosome covers two codons, AAA and GCU; tRNAs with anticodons UUU (carrying lysine) and CGA (carrying alanine) pair with them by complementary bases, the growing chain Met-Lys is transferred, and the ribosome moves one codon at a time until the stop codon UAG, giving Met-Lys-Ala-Trp-His.
caption: Figure: codon-anticodon pairing at the ribosome during elongation

alt: Two conducting tissues compared: a xylem vessel is a dead empty tube with lignin rings, pits and no end walls, so water flows as a continuous column; phloem has living sieve tube elements joined by sieve plates with no nucleus and little cytoplasm, next to a companion cell with a nucleus and many mitochondria connected by plasmodesmata.
caption: Figure: structure of a xylem vessel and of phloem (sieve tube elements with a companion cell)
